newsitem.title: USA: AT&T puts investors on hold, again.
newsitem.headline: AT&T puts investors on hold, again.

text.p: AT&T Corp. on Monday said its plans to enter new local telephone and wireless markets will come with an expensive price tag and that its earnings would be hurt by the substantial investments.
It also said it would cut $2.6 billion in costs, but said there would be no additional job cuts.

At the opening of a two-day meeting with analysts, AT&T officials said plans to compete in the core long-distance business, and in new areas such as local service, wireless communications and information services, would require investments of $8 billion to $9 billion in this year alone.

"In the short-term, the investments will put increasing strain on our financial performance," AT&T Chairman Robert Allen said. "These investments put AT&T on a path for powerful growth, but there's no question that they will dilute earnings in the near term."
The news sent the stock tumbling $3 to $36.875 in composite trading of nearly 10 million shares.
"It was somewhat of a shock," said Richard Toole, an analyst at Merrill Lynch.
But analysts said that AT&T, by announcing the $2.6 billion of cost cuts over the next two years, seemed to be clearing the decks for a later improvement in earnings.
AT&T set itself a five-year target of earning $5-$6 per share, compared with $5.6 billion, or $3.47 a share, from continuing operations in 1996.
It said 1997 earnings from core long-distance and wireless businesses would be only $3.45 to $3.75, even before the cost of new investments.
At the meeting, AT&T officials said new growth initiatives in local calling and wireless expansion would cost the company an additional 75 cents to $1 per share in 1997.
In 1996, these investments cost the company 59 cents per share when subtracted from the $4.06 per share AT&T earned from core businesses.
"The earnings targets are incredibly low compared to what we expected," said Frank Governali of CS First Boston.
Analysts had been expecting $3.25 to $3.45 per share, including all costs.
The meeting with analysts at AT&T headquarters was the first for President John Walter with Wall Street analysts since he took the post of president and chief operating officer.
AT&T officials said first-quarter 1997 earnings could be as much as 10 percent below the $1.2 billion, or 76 cents per share, reported in last year's fourth quarter.

AT&T has been facing increasing competitive pressure, not just from traditional rivals like MCI Communications Corp. and Sprint Corp., but also from a host of tiny, aggressive resellers who use AT&T's own networks to compete against it.
In addition, it faces the threat of regional Bells that are hoping to enter long distance markets in force this year.
AT&T said the $2.6 billion in expense reductions would come over the next two years, and that a portion of this figure was reflected in the new 1997 earnings target.

However, it emphasised that there will be no job cuts beyond the 11,200 it plans to make by the end of 1998. In January 1996, AT&T laid out a plan to cut 17,000 jobs in three years. It has so far cut 5,800.
"There was a real emphasis on cost-cutting," said Toole.

"The company is balancing on a very tricky razor's edge," said David Roddy, chief telecommunications economist for the consulting group Deloitte & Touche. "At the same time AT&T is planning big cost-cuts, the company is also talking about its ingenious entry into new markets," he said.

In order to compete in new areas like local service, wireless and Internet, AT&T will have to hire knowledgeable people -- a tough act when the company also is committed to reducing costs and the number of outside consultants it hires.
AT&T's plan is to provide a bundle of services that will keep customers loyal across a range of long distance, wireless and local calling services in the future.
It also plans to speed up its reaction to marketplace developments.
"The rate of change inside AT&T must be faster than the rate of change outside," said Walter.
